text:
**The Benchmark**

The road over Sunlight Pass is not much of a road after the first of October. The county stops grading it, and the snowplows, when they come at all, give up at the cattle guard below the switchbacks. Hollis Marr walked it most afternoons anyway, because a cardiologist in Billings had told him to walk somewhere every day, and he had taken the instruction more literally than intended. He was sixty-three, four years retired from the Bureau of Land Management.

He found the car a little after three, on a bend above the creek. He saw the tire marks first, two dark arcs in the gravel that ran straight where the road curved, and he looked at them the way he would have looked at a moved survey stake, with a kind of professional irritation, before he understood what they meant.

The car was a green Subaru. It had gone sixty feet down the slope and come to rest on its roof against a pair of trees. One rear wheel was still turning, very slowly, in the wind. That was the detail he would remember later: not the woman, not the glass, but the wheel, which seemed the last part of the event still happening.

He went down sideways, holding on to saplings. A woman hung upside down in her seat belt, her hair falling toward the roof. He said, "Ma'am," then louder, then reached in and put two fingers against her neck, the way he had been taught in a first-aid course in 1987, and held them there longer than he needed to. Her skin was cool, the temperature of a room no one has been in all day.

He climbed back up and walked toward the ridge until his phone found one bar. The dispatcher was a young man who said "Okay" after everything, as though checking items off a list. Okay, single vehicle. Okay, no signs of life. Okay, sir, a deputy and an ambulance are coming out of Cody, but that's an hour and a half, maybe two.

"You don't have to stay with the vehicle," the dispatcher said. "If you can give us a mile marker."

"There aren't any mile markers up here."

"Okay," the dispatcher said.

---

He went back down. It was not a decision so much as the absence of a reason to do anything else. His house in Crandall was eleven miles away and contained a cold woodstove and a refrigerator holding half an onion and a jar of horseradish. Up here was a woman who had been alive this morning and who would otherwise be alone in a ditch until strangers came for her, and it seemed someone should be with her in the interval.

He sat on a fallen log six feet from the open window, where he could see her hand. It was a capable-looking hand, with short nails and a silver ring on the thumb.

On the ceiling of the car lay the things that had been on the seats: a coffee cup, a dog leash, a water bowl, a canvas bag, and a library book, *Lichens of North America*. He leaned forward to read the slip tucked in the front. Due October 14th. Nine days.

"Well," he said aloud. "They'll waive the fine, I'd think."

His voice sounded strange in the trees. He had lived alone long enough that he sometimes went days without speaking. But having started, it was easier to go on.

"My mother used to scrape lichens off the gravestones. In Iowa. Every Memorial Day she'd go out with a brush and clean up the family. I told her it was a losing battle. She said everything was a losing battle, and you fought it anyway, or you weren't paying attention."

A raven on a snag across the drainage made a sound like a stick knocked against a hollow log.

---

He thought of the leash then, and stood and whistled into the trees, two notes, rising. Nothing came. The wind moved in the lodgepoles with a sound like distant traffic. The dog might be dead somewhere he couldn't see, or might have run off, and he didn't know which he'd prefer, and was ashamed to be making the calculation.

"Maybe he's home," he said, sitting down again. "Somebody's feeding him."

He told her about surveying, because it was what he knew. For thirty-one years he had set monuments, brass disks cemented into bedrock to mark a point whose latitude and elevation had been measured and agreed upon. They had his initials stamped on the face. When he was young he had felt a kind of pride in it, writing his name on the mountains.

"But they move," he said. "The whole continent moves, a couple of inches a year out here. Every so often the government re-measures everything, and all the numbers change. The disk is still in the rock. It just isn't where it says it is anymore." He turned a pinecone over in his hands. "I set one on Pilot Peak in 1991. Bet it's moved three feet. It still says the same thing, though. It doesn't know."

---

The light went off the high peaks after five, and the cold came down out of the timber like something poured. Down the drainage an elk bugled, a long rusty whine that always sounded to him like a gate opening somewhere far away.

As it got darker he became aware of the size of the country in a way he had not been in years. When you walked every day in a place you stopped seeing it. Now it reasserted itself: the black ridge across the creek, the unmeasured miles of timber running north into the Beartooths, no light anywhere but his phone, which he turned off to save the battery. The mountains had not noticed the car going over and would not notice it being hauled out. That was not frightening, exactly. It was closer to restful.

"My daughter buried a bird once," he said, after a long silence. "She was six. A cedar waxwing hit our window in Rock Springs. We put it in a shoebox by the fence and she said a few words. The next morning she dug it up to see if it was still there." He laughed a little in the dark. "It was. She was very disappointed. She thought it would have gone somewhere." He paused. "She's a nurse in Portland now. We talk at Christmas. It's not anybody's fault. We drifted, like the benchmarks. You look up one day and the numbers don't match."

He thought about walking up to the ridge to call her. But he could not think what he would say that would not alarm her, and it was a Tuesday, and she would be at work.

---

He had been married nineteen years to a woman named Joanne, who left in 1998 and died in 2016 in Denver, with her second husband beside her. A cousin had mailed him the obituary, folded in thirds. What struck him, reading it at his mailbox, was that he had gone about his days for eight months without knowing she was dying. The world had arranged itself around her absence before he had learned to expect it.

He told the woman in the car about this, perhaps because she was the first person in a long time to whom he could say anything without watching their face.

"Somebody right now doesn't know about you," he said. "Somebody's making dinner. They're still living in the world where you're alive. I'm the only one who's crossed over into the other one. It's a strange thing to be the only one."

Somewhere in the car, he realized, a phone had been buzzing, intermittently, for some time.

---

The headlights came at a quarter to seven. He climbed up, knees cracking, and waved his arms.

The deputy was a heavyset woman with reading glasses on a cord. She shone her flashlight down the slope and said, "Jesus," quietly. "You been here this whole time?"

"Yes."

She looked at him a moment longer than necessary. "You didn't have to do that. Dispatch should've told you."

"They did."

The paramedics went down with a stretcher and a brisk, practiced gentleness he could not watch. When the deputy asked what time he'd found the vehicle, he said a little after three, and when she asked how he knew, he said it was just where the sun was.

"There's a dog," he said. "Maybe. There's a leash in the car."

"We'll put it out. Somebody'll keep an eye."

She offered to drive him home. He said he would walk. She said it was eleven miles and below freezing, and in the end he let her, because he was more tired than he had been in years.

---

As the truck pulled away he looked back once at the lights moving among the trees. Then they came around the bend and there was only the road unspooling in the headlights, and the dark country on either side, unmeasured, indifferent, enormous.

Somewhere back there, a book was nine days from being due. A phone was ringing in a canvas bag. A disk with his initials on it was moving, imperceptibly, toward the Pacific. And something, maybe a dog, maybe not, was moving through the timber in the dark, toward a road where it had last seen someone it knew. He hoped it would find what it was looking for. He hoped, at least, that someone would be there.
